DZA: It's the largest country in Africa by area, and over 80% of it is covered by the Sahara.
Its flag's red crescent and star sit on a field split green and white.
The ancient Roman city of Timgad here is so well preserved it's called the 'Pompeii of Africa'.
AGO: It was a Portuguese colony until 1975, so Portuguese is still its official language.
Kalandula Falls here is one of the largest waterfalls in Africa by volume.
Its exclave of Cabinda is cut off from the rest of the country by a strip of DR Congo.
BEN: It's considered the birthplace of Vodun (Voodoo), which is an officially recognised religion here.
The Kingdom of Dahomey here was famous for its all-female army, the Agojie.
Its official capital is Porto-Novo, but the government mostly sits in Cotonou.
BWA: The Okavango Delta here is one of the world's largest inland deltas — the river never reaches the sea.
It has the world's largest population of African elephants, roughly 130,000.
It's one of the world's biggest diamond producers, which turned it from one of the poorest countries into a middle-income one.
BFA: Its name means 'land of upright (honest) people' in a mix of Mooré and Dyula.
Its capital Ouagadougou hosts FESPACO, Africa's largest film festival.
It used to be called Upper Volta, after the Volta River.
BDI: It's one of the few African countries whose borders match a pre-colonial kingdom.
Lake Tanganyika, on its border, is the world's second-deepest lake.
Its royal drummers perform a ritual drumming tradition listed by UNESCO.
CPV: It's an archipelago of 10 volcanic islands about 570 km off West Africa.
Singer Cesária Évora, the 'barefoot diva', made its morna music world-famous.
Pico do Fogo here is an active volcano that last erupted in 2014.
CMR: It's nicknamed 'Africa in miniature' because it has deserts, rainforests, mountains and savanna.
Mount Cameroon, an active volcano, is the highest peak in West and Central Africa.
It has both English and French as official languages, a legacy of British and French rule.
CAF: It's one of the most landlocked countries on Earth — far from any coast.
The Dzanga-Sangha reserve here has forest elephants and western lowland gorillas.
Its name simply describes where it is on the continent.
TCD: It's named after Lake Chad, which has shrunk by about 90% since the 1960s.
The Ennedi Plateau here is full of sandstone arches and ancient rock art.
Its flag is almost identical to Romania's — the blue is just a shade darker.
COM: It's an archipelago in the Indian Ocean known as the 'Perfume Islands' for its ylang-ylang.
The coelacanth, a fish thought extinct for 66 million years, was rediscovered in its waters.
It has experienced around 20 coups or coup attempts since independence in 1975.
COG: Its capital Brazzaville sits directly across the Congo River from Kinshasa — the closest pair of capitals in the world (apart from Rome and Vatican City).
Over 60% of the country is covered by rainforest.
It's often called Congo-Brazzaville to tell it apart from its much larger neighbour.
COD: It's the second-largest country in Africa and the largest French-speaking country by population.
The Congo River here is the deepest river in the world, over 220 m deep in places.
It produces about 70% of the world's cobalt, used in phone and EV batteries.
DJI: Lake Assal here is the lowest point in Africa, 155 m below sea level, and saltier than the Dead Sea.
It hosts military bases of the US, France, China, Japan and others thanks to its strategic spot on the Bab-el-Mandeb strait.
Its capital has the same name as the country.
EGY: The Great Pyramid of Giza here is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing.
About 95% of the population lives within a few kilometres of the Nile.
The Suez Canal here links the Mediterranean and Red Sea, carrying about 12% of world trade.
GNQ: It's the only country in Africa with Spanish as an official language.
Its capital, Malabo, is on an island (Bioko), not the mainland.
Oil made it one of Africa's richest countries per person, though wealth is very unevenly spread.
ERI: Its capital Asmara is a UNESCO site for its 1930s Italian modernist architecture, including a building shaped like an airplane.
It gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993 after a 30-year war.
The Danakil Depression, partly in its territory, is one of the hottest places on Earth.
SWZ: It's one of the last absolute monarchies in the world.
In 2018 the king renamed it from Swaziland to its current name.
It's one of the smallest countries in Africa, almost completely surrounded by South Africa.
ETH: It was never colonised (apart from a brief Italian occupation from 1936–41).
It uses its own calendar, which is about 7–8 years behind the Gregorian one, with 13 months.
Coffee is believed to have originated here, in the region of Kaffa.
GAB: About 88% of the country is covered by rainforest.
Its Loango National Park is famous for 'surfing hippos' that swim in the ocean.
Natural nuclear fission reactors that ran 2 billion years ago were found at Oklo here.
GMB: It's the smallest country on mainland Africa — a thin strip along a river, surrounded by Senegal.
Its borders follow the river, supposedly set by how far a British gunboat's cannon could fire.
It's nicknamed 'the Smiling Coast of Africa'.
GHA: In 1957 it became the first sub-Saharan African colony to gain independence.
Lake Volta here is one of the largest artificial lakes in the world by surface area.
It's one of the world's top cocoa producers, along with neighbouring Côte d'Ivoire.
GIN: It's called the 'water tower of West Africa' because the Niger, Senegal and Gambia rivers all start here.
It holds about a quarter of the world's known bauxite (aluminium ore) reserves.
Its capital Conakry was originally built on an island.
GNB: The Bijagós Archipelago here has saltwater hippos and is a UNESCO biosphere reserve.
Cashew nuts make up the vast majority of its exports.
It shares part of its name with two other countries.
CIV: The Basilica of Our Lady of Peace in Yamoussoukro is one of the largest churches in the world.
It's the world's biggest cocoa producer, growing about 40% of the global supply.
Its government asks that the country's name not be translated into other languages.
KEN: Its runners have won more Olympic medals in long-distance events than almost any other country.
The Great Migration of over a million wildebeest crosses into its Maasai Mara each year.
M-Pesa, the mobile money service launched here in 2007, pioneered banking by text message.
LSO: It's completely surrounded by South Africa — one of only three countries enclosed by a single other country.
Its lowest point is about 1,400 m above sea level, the highest low point of any country.
Its people traditionally wear a woven conical hat called a mokorotlo, which appears on its flag.
LBR: It's Africa's oldest republic, founded in 1847 by freed American slaves.
Its flag looks like the US flag, but with one big star.
Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, elected here in 2005, was Africa's first elected female head of state.
LBY: Over 90% of the country is desert.
Al-'Aziziyah here once held the world temperature record, which was later invalidated.
It has the largest proven oil reserves in Africa.
MDG: About 90% of its wildlife is found nowhere else on Earth, including all wild lemurs.
It's the fourth-largest island in the world.
It produces most of the world's natural vanilla.
MWI: Lake Malawi has more fish species than any other lake on Earth — over 700 kinds of cichlid.
It's nicknamed 'the Warm Heart of Africa' for the friendliness of its people.
The lake makes up about a fifth of the country's total area.
MLI: Timbuktu here was a great centre of Islamic learning, with hundreds of thousands of ancient manuscripts.
The Great Mosque of Djenné is the largest mud-brick building in the world.
Mansa Musa, a 14th-century emperor here, is often called the richest person in history.
MRT: The Richat Structure, or 'Eye of the Sahara', is a 40 km-wide circular formation visible from space.
One of the world's longest trains, up to 2.5 km long, carries iron ore across the desert here.
In 1981 it became the last country in the world to abolish slavery.
MUS: It was the only known home of the dodo, which went extinct in the late 1600s.
Its 'underwater waterfall' is an optical illusion of sand flowing off an undersea shelf.
It had no native human population before Europeans arrived.
MAR: The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, founded in 859, is the oldest continuously operating university in the world.
It's only about 14 km from Europe across the Strait of Gibraltar.
The city of Chefchaouen is famous for having almost every wall painted blue.
MOZ: Its flag is the only national flag with a modern rifle (an AK-47) on it.
It has a coastline of about 2,500 km along the Indian Ocean.
It's one of the few Commonwealth members that was never a British colony.
NAM: The Namib Desert here is considered the oldest desert in the world, at least 55 million years old.
It was the first country to write environmental protection into its constitution.
Sossusvlei's red dunes are among the tallest in the world, some over 300 m high.
NER: It has the youngest population in the world, with a median age of around 15.
Over 80% of the country lies within the Sahara.
It's named after the river that flows through its southwest.
NGA: It's the most populous country in Africa, with over 220 million people.
Its film industry, Nollywood, makes more films a year than Hollywood.
RWA: It's known as the 'Land of a Thousand Hills'.
It has the highest share of women in parliament of any country — over 60%.
Plastic bags have been banned here since 2008.
STP: It's the second-smallest country in Africa, after the Seychelles.
It was once the world's largest cocoa producer, in the early 1900s.
The equator passes through one of its small islands, Ilhéu das Rolas.
SEN: Dakar here is the westernmost city on mainland Africa.
Lake Retba is famously pink because of salt-loving algae.
It was the finish line of the Paris–Dakar Rally for decades.
SYC: It's Africa's smallest country by both area and population.
The coco de mer palm here produces the world's largest seed, up to 25 kg.
Its capital, Victoria, is one of the smallest capitals in the world.
SLE: Its capital, Freetown, was founded as a settlement for freed slaves.
It's a major source of diamonds, including some of the largest ever found.
Its natural harbour is one of the largest in the world.
SOM: It has the longest coastline of any country on mainland Africa.
It's estimated to have more camels than any other country, around 7 million.
Nearly everyone here speaks the same language, which is unusual for Africa.
ZAF: It has three capital cities: Pretoria, Cape Town and Bloemfontein.
It has 12 official languages, including sign language.
The world's first human heart transplant was performed in Cape Town in 1967.
SSD: It's the world's newest country, gaining independence in 2011.
The Sudd here is one of the largest wetlands in the world.
Its people include the Dinka, among the tallest populations on Earth.
SDN: It has more pyramids than Egypt — over 200, built by the Kingdom of Kush.
The Blue Nile and White Nile meet at its capital, Khartoum.
It was the largest country in Africa until its southern part split off in 2011.
TZA: Mount Kilimanjaro here is the highest mountain in Africa, at 5,895 m.
It includes the island of Zanzibar, once a centre of the spice trade.
The Olduvai Gorge here is one of the most important sites for early human fossils.
TGO: It's long and thin — about 580 km from north to south, but at most around 160 km wide.
Its capital Lomé has a famous fetish market selling items for traditional medicine.
The mud tower-houses of the Batammariba people here are a UNESCO site.
TUN: The ruins of ancient Carthage are just outside its capital.
Parts of Star Wars were filmed here, and a desert town gave its name to the planet Tatooine.
UGA: It's home to about half of the world's remaining mountain gorillas.
Lake Victoria, Africa's largest lake, is one of the sources of the Nile.
Winston Churchill called it 'the Pearl of Africa'.
ZMB: Victoria Falls on its border is one of the largest waterfalls in the world, known locally as 'the Smoke That Thunders'.
It's one of Africa's largest copper producers.
It was formerly called Northern Rhodesia.
ZWE: Great Zimbabwe, a medieval stone city here, gave the country its name.
In 2008 it suffered hyperinflation so extreme it printed a 100-trillion-dollar note.
It shares Victoria Falls with its northern neighbour.
